exercises.label: Sense Memory
exercises.basis: Recreating a remembered object or sensation until feeling follows is Lee Strasberg's sense-memory exercise, which he developed from Stanislavski's 'emotion memory' chapter. The name and the method are Strasberg's, not Stanislavski's.

exercises.label: The Repetition Exercise
exercises.basis: Meisner's repetition exercise, accurately described.

exercises.label: The Given Circumstances
exercises.basis: Stanislavski's given circumstances and magic if, written out in the who/where/when/what-do-I-want form of Hagen's character questions. A standard homework task, but not a single named exercise.

exercises.label: Circles Of Attention
exercises.basis: Stanislavski's small, medium and large circles of attention, from 'Concentration of Attention' in An Actor Prepares.

exercises.label: A Recall Drill
exercises.basis: Retrieval practice from Roediger & Karpicke (2006) applied to learning a speech by its meaning (Noice & Noice 2006). Both are laboratory findings; no actor-training text names this drill. The label 'A Recall Drill' already reads as generic.

exercises.label: Adjustments
exercises.basis: Replaying a speech under changing adjustments is common studio practice, and 'adjustment' is Meisner-technique vocabulary. The cited source, Johnstone's 'accepting offers', is about accepting a partner's offer in improvisation, not reworking a speech under a note. The attribution is weak; Meisner would be the closer source.

exercises.label: Voice Work
exercises.basis: Breath, release and resonance, then text on the breath: a generic voice warm-up in the Linklater/Berry tradition, not one named exercise.

exercises.label: Movement Work
exercises.basis: Laban effort work through the four motion factors (space, weight, time, flow) is real Laban practice; moving from there to a character's walk is a common studio extension.

exercises.label: Dialect Drill
exercises.basis: Working from a recorded native speaker through sound changes and the music of the accent is standard dialect coaching. Yale's Speech and Accents sequence exists.

exercises.label: Audition Pieces
exercises.basis: Two contrasting monologues is the standard audition requirement. DRAM 743b exists, though its description stresses sides and a reader rather than monologues.

exercises.label: Character Work
exercises.basis: Joins named techniques: Chekhov's psychological gesture and imaginary centre, and animal work, a conservatory staple that is not Chekhov's.

exercises.label: Verse Speaking
exercises.basis: Scansion, line endings and antithesis is standard Shakespeare verse work (Berry, and also Barton's Playing Shakespeare). DRAM 203 exists and is about heightened language.

exercises.label: Clown Practice
exercises.basis: Lecoq red-nose clown work. The 'flop' is Lecoq's 'le bide'; entrances in the nose are a standard clown-class exercise.

exercises.label: Cold Reading
exercises.basis: Cold reading of unseen sides is standard audition-class practice and matches DRAM 743b's description (sides, reader, real-time adjustments).

exercises.label: Comic Timing
exercises.basis: Bergson's Laughter is a philosophical theory of the comic ('the mechanical encrusted on the living') and holds no timing exercise. The set-up/pause/turn drill is SLATE's own framing of common rehearsal practice and should be labelled as the game's own, with Bergson as background at most.

exercises.label: A Dance Class
exercises.basis: Barre, centre and combination is the standard structure of a ballet or jazz technique class. But the cited Yale courses (The Body as Source, DRAM 133/233) are not dance classes (see citations).

exercises.label: An Improv Session
exercises.basis: Scenes from a suggestion, accepting offers: standard improvisation practice in the Johnstone and Spolin traditions.

exercises.label: Intimacy Practice
exercises.basis: Boundaries, consent and choreographed intimacy are the tools of contemporary intimacy direction. DRAM 403 covers 'theatrical violence and intimacy'.

exercises.label: Self-Tape Practice
exercises.basis: Self-taping and reviewing playback is current industry practice. DRAM 463 films scenes and watches them back.

exercises.label: Scene Work
exercises.basis: Beats (Stanislavski's units), objectives and playable actions: standard scene-study method.

exercises.label: Script Analysis
exercises.basis: Events, through-line and superobjective: standard textual analysis built on Stanislavski's terms. The RADA 'textual strand' phrase was not found.

exercises.label: Singing Practice
exercises.basis: Scales, then a song worked for acting and notes: standard voice-studio and acting-through-song practice. DRAM 413/423 exist.

exercises.label: Speech Drill
exercises.basis: Articulation drills, then a speech for clarity at size: standard speech training. 'Standard American speech' is not in the DRAM 123 description and was not verified as Yale's approach.

exercises.label: Combat Drill
exercises.basis: Footwork, falls and unarmed technique at half then full speed is standard stage-combat training. The unarmed work is DRAM 403; 405 is armed.

exercises.label: Copy Reading
exercises.basis: Reading commercial and narration copy to a microphone and listening back is ordinary voice-over practice. The code already says it has no published curriculum behind it, which is accurate.
exercises.source: none (the code cites none, and none was sought)

summary: abilities.ts attributes the quotation 'improvement is rapid at first but decreases as the practitioner becomes more skilled' to Ericsson et al. (1993). It is the opening sentence of Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000), p. 185. It does not appear in Ericsson et al.

abilities.ts (stamina) says Hickson et al. found aerobic gains 'halve in 10 to 11 days'. The paper reports half-times of the increase of 10.3 and 10.8 days: half the gain is made in that time. The plateau at three weeks is correct.

engagement.ts credits the 'sixth play' satiation figure to Galak, Kruger & Loewenstein (2011). Galak et al. report it from Ratner, Kahn & Kahneman (1999). The 'gap restores it' finding is Galak et al.'s own.

Edition mismatches: Berry's 1987 book was 'The Actor and His Text' ('The Actor and the Text' is the 1992 retitling). Laban's 1950 book was 'The Mastery of Movement on the Stage' ('The Mastery of Movement' is the 1960 second edition).

Yale citations: every course code, title and teacher in school.ts matches the 2026-2027 bulletin. Two practice.ts uses misfit the course descriptions. 'A Dance Class' (barre, centre, combination) cites The Body as Source (DRAM 133/233), which is energetic-body work, not a dance class. 'Combat Drill' (unarmed) cites DRAM 405, which is armed combat; the unarmed work is DRAM 403.

Exercise labelling: 'Comic Timing' (sourced to Bergson's theory) and 'A Recall Drill' (a lab finding applied) are SLATE's own and should say so. 'Adjustments' is sourced to Johnstone's accepting offers, which does not describe it; Meisner's adjustments would be closer. 'Sense Memory' is Strasberg's exercise, built on Stanislavski's emotion memory. Repetition (Meisner) and Circles of Attention (Stanislavski) are accurately named pedagogy exercises.

Everything else checked was verified, figure included: Roediger & Karpicke 61% vs 40%; Macnamara et al. 21%/18%; Ericsson et al. ~4 h/day, 2 h, 7,410 h; Heathcote et al.; Bennett et al. -.39/-.35/-.18; Hunter et al. 21.3%/h; de Witte et al. d = .380/.545; Frattaroli r = .075; Reeves et al. -1.39/-1.41; LAMDA 50/65/80; Hidi & Renninger; Costa & McCrae; Arthur et al.; Mujika & Padilla; Clow & Fredhoi; Bratman et al.; Lim & Dinges; Noice & Noice.
Not fully verified: the Clow & Fredhoi issue number; Bratman et al.'s volume and pages, which come from memory; RADA's 'textual strand' wording; 'standard American speech' as Yale's DRAM 123 content.
